hook: You tapped your card, you got your points, and you walked away feeling smart.
But in the two seconds that card touched the machine, at least three companies got paid.
The card company makes money from you, whether you pay your bill on time or not.
Today, we're opening up the machine to see exactly how.
t1: When you tap, the coffee shop doesn't receive $5,
The difference is a swipe fee, and the biggest piece of it is called interchange.
Interchange goes to the bank that issued your card.
On a credit card, that's usually around 2-3% of the purchase.
On a $5 coffee, that's 10 or 15 cents.
Now multiply it by every card, every purchase, every day.
In 2025, US merchants paid a record of roughly $198 billion in card swipe fees.
US banks alone collected nearly $66 billion in interchange that year,
about 11% of all their non-interest income.
And who really pays for it?
The coffee shop builds that cost into its prices,
so even people paying with cash are quietly helping fund the system.
t2: Swipe fees are the quiet money. Interest is the loud money. If you don't pay your full balance by
the due date, the bank charges you interest on what's left. Right now, U.S. credit card accounts
that carry a balance pay around 22% a year on average, according to Federal Reserve data.
Store cards are often even higher. Here's what that looks like. Say Leo carries a $5,000 balance
all year. At 22%, that's roughly $1,100 or more in interest, money that buys him absolutely
nothing. Now zoom out. In 2024, card companies charged Americans about $160 billion in interest.
Two years earlier, it was $105 billion. That's the engine.
t3: So what about cashback and travel points? Isn't the bank giving money back?
This is where it gets interesting. The U.S. Consumer Financial Protection Bureau
looked at major card companies and found a striking split. People who carried a balance
month to month paid 94% of all interest and fees, but they earned only 27% of the rewards.
People who paid in full every month paid just 6% of the interest and fees,
and collected 73% of the rewards. In other words, rewards are partly funded by swipe fees,
and partly funded by the people who are struggling.
The free points in one wallet are often paid for by the interest in another.
t4: None of this happens by accident. Look at your statement. The biggest, friendliest number is
often the minimum payment. It feels manageable, but paying only the minimum keeps most of the
balance alive, and that balance keeps earning interest for the bank. This matters because
more people are doing it. The CFPB found that in 2024, 15% of general purpose cardholders
made only the minimum payment, the highest level in at least a decade. Then there are the fees:
late fees, cash advance fees, balance transfer fees, annual fees. Each one is small on its own.
Together, they add up to tens of billions of dollars a year.
cust: From the bank's point of view, there are roughly three kinds of customers.
The first pays in full every month.
The bank earns swipe fees from them, but pays out rewards.
Some industry insiders have a nickname for them, deadbeats,
not because they're bad with money, but because they don't pay interest.
The second carries a balance and pays steadily.
This is the most profitable customer.
They pay the most in fees, but they're also the riskiest,
because if they stop paying, the bank loses.
The whole business is a balancing act between these three doors.
mean: So is a credit card good or bad? Neither. It's a tool, and it was designed by people who understand
money very well. Once you understand how it earns, you can decide for yourself which door you're
walking through. Everyone's situation is different, so if you're making a big decision,
outro: Next time you tap your card, you'll know.
